newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Mir chief's mum prays for return from damaged ship.
newsitem.headline: Mir chief's mum prays for return from damaged ship.

text.p: As the commander of Russia's crippled Mir orbital station grappled with problems in outer space, his mother had more down-to-earth concerns about a ship she said her son told her was long overdue for a refit.
"The only thing I want and pray to God for it is that Vasily comes back alive and healthy," Valentina Tsibliyeva told Reuters in a weekend interview, sitting in her tiny whitewashed yard.

When he returns -- in mid-August according to the latest plans after he developed a heart problem -- his mother will be able to tell Vasily Tsibliyev for the first time that his beloved stepfather died of a heart attack four months ago.

Problems have plagued Tsibliyev's mission, starting with a fire after he and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin went aboard Mir in February and culminating in the station's worst ever accident when a cargo ship the commander was manoevring by remote control slammed into one of its modules and punctured it.
Since the crash on June 25, a mystery liquid leaked into space, stress gave Tsibliyev a heart problem and Mir's computer crashed when one of the three crewmen pulled out the wrong cable.
Sharp words have passed between Mission Control and the crew. Ground experts will neither confirm nor deny reports Tsibliyev was to blame for the collision.
The commander's mother, though, has no doubts the blame lay with the ageing technology of the 11-year-old station.

"I think it wasn't the cosmonauts' fault. This was an oversight on Earth. He told me before that they should have repaired the station ages ago. Otherwise it would just crash at some point," the 64-year-old pensioner said.
"Now he has overstrained his heart," she added.

"He never complained about his health. I am worried but believed his heart problem was not very serious. I think he won't fly in space any more," she added, sitting under a spreading nut tree by a garden of raspberries and parsley.
The mission doctor said on Monday that Tsibliyev's irregular heartbeat, first noticed a week ago, had become normal following a course of sedatives and heart pills.
Valentina still lives in the same house where Tsibliyev was born 43 years ago and where he lived in childhood poverty.

There is no running water, the refrigerator is broken and only her garden and monthly pension of $20 support her in the village of Orekhovka, inhabited mostly by ethnic Russians 170 km (95 miles) east of the city of Simferopol on Ukraine's Crimea peninsula.

For news of her son, she borrows a neighbour's telephone to call her daughter-in-law Larisa in Moscow. She also goes to the neighbours to watch television every day to know what is going on with her boy, hundreds of kilometres above the Earth.

"Vasily dreamed about becoming a pilot since he was just a very small boy. He thought of nothing else. He drew pictures of planes -- and every time in his air battles our side won against the enemies," she recalls. "I kept telling him 'Vasya, you can't always win. That's life.'"
Tsibliyev flew Soviet MiG-21 fighter jets from bases in East Germany and Moldova after qualifying from the Kharkiv aviation school and then took further qualifications in Moscow.
"He always tried to hide his real plans. He thought I never guessed his aim was to be not just a pilot, but a cosmonaut.
"I knew the idea to go into outer space came to him immediately after Gagarin's flight," she said. Russian Yuri Gagarin became the first man in space in 1961.
The mother of the man at the forefront of manned space flight complains about her health, particulary a bad heart, and especially that she does not have enough money for medicines.
She has yet to tell Tsibliyev of the death of his stepfather, also named Vasily.

"His stepfather was like a father to him. They never had a quarrel," Valentina said. "He doesn't know his father is no longer alive. How can I tell him if he is in space, especially when not everything's all right up there? It'll make things harder for him. I'll tell him when he lands and recovers."
Her favourite pastime is looking at old family photos, and those of Vasily training during the years prior to this and his earlier space missions. And reading old letters, too.
"Mum, don't worry, everything will be fine because you brought me up in the best way, and I was well-trained for the mission," he wrote from the Baikonur cosmodrome in 1993.
"I am sure I chose this path and this fate correctly because I cannnot imagine not doing this job," he added.
"See you on our native, beautiful and beloved Earth."
